q: First Aid is the definitive and later care for trauma and acute illness patients.
e: First aid is immediate initial assistance. Definitive treatment is provided by qualified health professionals.

q: First aid intervention is mainly used to save lives.
e: First aid aims to preserve life, prevent deterioration, and promote recovery.

q: Artificial respiration is to facilitate flow of air into the lung from an environment only.
e: Artificial ventilation helps move air into and out of the lungs, not just one way.

q: CPR is mainly used only to restore circulation.
e: CPR uses chest compressions and, when appropriate, rescue breaths to support circulation and oxygen delivery.

q: During basic life support, checking scene safety is the first activity.
e: Check the scene for danger before approaching, then assess responsiveness and call for emergency help.

q: If signs of circulation exist but there is no breathing, immediately start CPR.
e: If a pulse is present but breathing is absent, provide rescue breathing according to your training and monitor the pulse. CPR is needed when circulation is absent.

q: There is no risk during mouth-to-mouth breathing because it is life-saving.
e: Rescue breathing can involve infection risk. Use a barrier device when available and follow current training.

q: For penetrating abdominal injuries, the best first aid is replacing protruding organs.
e: Never push exposed organs back inside. Cover loosely with a sterile dressing moistened with sterile saline if available, and get emergency help.

q: A closed fracture is a broken bone associated with an open wound.
e: A closed fracture does not break through the skin. An open fracture has a wound communicating with the fracture.

q: A strain is overstretching or tearing of muscles or tendons, for example during heavy lifting.
e: A strain affects muscle or tendon; a sprain affects a ligament.

q: Why do you give first aid to the injured woman with massive bleeding?
e: All three are key aims of first aid: preserve life, prevent deterioration, and promote recovery.

q: Which action is the best immediate priority for the patient with massive bleeding?
e: Apply firm direct pressure and get emergency help. Use a tourniquet for life-threatening limb bleeding if trained and indicated.

q: Which type of shock is she most likely to develop after massive blood loss?
e: Hypovolemic shock occurs when severe blood or fluid loss reduces circulating blood volume.

q: If she becomes irritable, dizzy, and confused, which listed vital sign can you check immediately?
e: Pulse rate is a vital sign and may become rapid in shock. Do not delay bleeding control or emergency care.

q: If she is unresponsive and has no pulse and no normal breathing, what should you do immediately?
o: Start CPR and activate emergency response
e: Activate emergency help, obtain an AED if available, and start CPR immediately.

q: Which action helps open the airway when spinal injury is not suspected?
e: Head tilt–chin lift opens the airway when trauma is not suspected. With suspected spinal injury, a trained rescuer may try jaw thrust while minimizing neck movement; opening the airway remains essential.

q: For an adult receiving conventional CPR, what is the standard compression-to-rescue-breath ratio?
e: For adult CPR, use 30 compressions followed by 2 breaths when trained and able to provide breaths.

q: A 24-year-old man has a lower right-leg fracture. What is the first-aid priority before definitive treatment?
e: Support and immobilize the limb in the position found, check circulation beyond the injury, and arrange urgent care. Do not attempt to straighten it.

q: After a fall where spinal injury is possible, which statement about opening the airway is most accurate?
o: Always use head lift and chin tilt
Use head tilt–chin lift in every case
A trained rescuer may use jaw thrust while minimizing neck movement
Point the chin down and head up
e: A trained rescuer may try jaw thrust. If it does not open the airway, use head tilt–chin lift because opening the airway is essential.

q: Which is NOT a recognized complication of chest compressions during CPR?
e: Rib or chest injuries and rarely internal injury can occur during CPR. Diarrhea is not a typical mechanical complication.

q: A decrease in blood pressure is called:
e: Hypotension means low blood pressure. Hypovolemia means reduced circulating blood volume and can cause hypotension.

q: The term tachycardia refers to:
e: Tachycardia means an abnormally fast heart rate. Tachypnea means an abnormally fast respiratory rate.

q: A 59-year-old woman falls and the bones at her knee joint appear displaced. What is the likely diagnosis?
e: A dislocation is displacement of the bones forming a joint. Do not attempt to put it back in place.

q: A woman has painful burns with edema and blisters involving the epidermis and part of the dermis. What is the burn depth?
e: Blisters and damage to the epidermis plus part of the dermis indicate a partial-thickness, commonly called second-degree, burn.

q: The burned areas are the right arm, right leg, and right half of the anterior chest. Using the exam’s apparent Rule of Nines estimate, what is the total body surface area burned?
e: The apparent estimate is right arm 9% + right leg 18% + half of the anterior chest about 4.5% = 31.5%. Exact estimates depend on the area actually burned.

q: Which is the appropriate first-aid approach for a thermal burn?
o: Cool with cool running water and cover loosely with a clean non-stick dressing
e: Cool a thermal burn with cool running water for about 20 minutes as soon as possible. Do not use ice, powders, oils, or break blisters.

q: Which type of shock can develop after a severe burn due to fluid loss?
e: Severe burns can cause major fluid shifts and loss, leading to hypovolemic shock.

q: A conscious patient swallowed kerosene 30 minutes ago. Which first-aid action is safest?
o: Give water to relieve stomach pain
Give milk to relieve stomach pain
Do not induce vomiting or give food/drink; get urgent poison or emergency advice
e: Kerosene can enter the lungs if vomited and cause serious injury. Do not induce vomiting or give anything by mouth unless poison specialists direct you.

q: Which feature normally occurs during exhalation (breathing out) at rest?
e: Quiet exhalation is usually passive: the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles relax, chest volume decreases, and air flows out.

q: Which can cause respiratory failure in an injured child?
o: The tongue falling back and obstructing the airway
e: Airway obstruction, trauma, and severe bleeding with shock can all threaten oxygen delivery and breathing.

q: A child has a sharp object penetrating the eye. Which statement is FALSE about first aid?
o: Do not try to remove the object
Do not press or wash the injured eye
Loosely cover both eyes to reduce eye movement, if possible without pressure
Secure the object without pressing on the eye and seek emergency care
e: Do not remove the object or press on the eye. Stabilize it with a protective shield and seek emergency care. Do not wash a penetrating injury.

q: A road-traffic injury causes a suspected ruptured eardrum with skull fracture and possible cerebrospinal fluid leakage. What is the correct first-aid approach?
o: Stop the fluid from coming out
Allow fluid to drain and loosely cover the ear without blocking it
Turn the injured person onto the injured side
e: Do not plug, clean, or try to stop possible cerebrospinal fluid leakage. Let it drain, cover loosely, minimize movement, and arrange emergency care.

g: PART II · FOREIGN BODY IN EYE
q: If you feel burning and suspect a loose particle in your eye, what is the safest first step?
o: Rinse gently with clean running water if no object is embedded
e: Do not rub or use instruments. Gentle irrigation may help a loose surface particle. If an object is embedded or vision changes, protect the eye and seek urgent care.

q: Which injuries commonly require a large bulk of dressing to pad and support the injured area?
o: Fractures of the femur and humerus
Fractures of the ankle and foot only
Fractures of the radius and ulna only
e: Large bones such as the femur and humerus may need substantial padding and support while immobilized. Obtain urgent medical care.

q: A small open wound on the scalp bleeds profusely. What is the specific injury called?
e: The scalp has a rich blood supply, so even a small scalp wound may bleed heavily. Avoid pressing directly over a suspected skull fracture or embedded object.
